messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame Osei, a 50-year-old plumber from Accra who had built a life in a midwestern American city, was assaulted eighteen months ago while leaving a late-night repair job. He had taken a shortcut through a dim parking lot behind a row of shops, carrying his tool bag, when a man came at him from behind, struck him in the head with a metal pipe, and took his wallet and phone. Kwame lay on the asphalt for several minutes before a security guard found him. He could not describe the attack in words afterward—when he tried, his mind offered only sharp, disjointed images: the glare of a streetlamp through his own blood, the weight of the pipe swinging, a boot near his face. The pictures came unbidden at any moment, especially at night, and each time they surfaced his chest tightened and he felt an overpowering shame. He was certain he should have seen it coming, should have been able to defend himself; the guilt that accompanied those visual memories corroded his sense of himself as a capable man.

In the weeks following the assault, Kwame tried to return to his trade. But the moment a client’s child darted around a corner or a coworker reached suddenly for a tool, his body locked and his heart hammered. He began to believe he was no longer the person who could handle the everyday chaos of a job site; the belief that he could not trust his own reactions meant that he felt unsafe in almost every space except his own house and the cab of his work van. His wife noticed he no longer agreed to evening calls, and he started turning down jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods, telling himself they were too risky. The feeling of injustice deepened—the police investigation went nowhere, and nothing had been done about the man who hurt him—and this bitterness fed a growing conviction that the world was fundamentally hostile, a place where he could not protect himself.

The visual memories kept returning, especially when he was alert and startled. He would be lying in bed, still wired from a minor flinch reaction during the day, and the image of the pipe swinging would flash into his mind, followed by a wave of guilt and helplessness. He had trouble falling asleep and often woke with a start, drenched in sweat. His wife tried to comfort him, but he could not explain what he was seeing; the memories refused to become a story he could tell, remaining only as pictures and sensations. Over the months, the connections tightened into a cycle he could not break: the more he felt incapable and robbed of justice, the more he scanned every room for hidden threats; the more he scanned, the more the intrusive images appeared; and each image reinforced his sense of being unsafe and permanently diminished.

His work suffered. He began missing appointments and lying to clients, saying he had too much on his plate. His wife grew frustrated with his withdrawal from social outings and his refusal to let their teenage son help with plumbing projects in the basement. Kwame knew he was disappointing his family, but he could not shake the certainty that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. It was his wife who finally convinced him to see a therapist, hoping he could reclaim the life he had lost. When he walked into the clinic, what frightened Kwame most was the possibility that the man he used to be—steady, confident, skilled—was gone for good, and that nothing could bring him back.
